title: Magnetic Particle Inspection for Oilfield Equipment | MPI
description: On-site magnetic particle inspection for US drilling and oilfield equipment: drill stem threads, hoisting gear, fluid ends and skid welds. Request a quote.
h1: Magnetic Particle Inspection for Oilfield and Drilling Equipment in the US
html:
Atlantis NDT performs magnetic particle inspection on United States onshore oilfield and drilling equipment: threaded connections on drill stem elements, hoisting equipment, rig structure welds, mud pump fluid ends, wellhead and treating iron, and welds on production skids. Technicians are mobilized to the rig yard, the pipe rack, the shop or the lease with yokes, wet suspension and portable lighting. Send the equipment list, the governing standard and the location, and request an MT inspection quote.

Why oilfield equipment cracks, and why MT is the first-choice method

Drilling and well-servicing equipment lives in fatigue. A drill string rotates while bent, a traveling block hoists loads that swing and shock, a mud pump fluid end sees pressure cycles measured in millions. Fatigue cracks start at the surface, usually at a stress raiser such as a thread root, a weld toe, a bore intersection or a corrosion pit, and grow quietly until the part fails. On ferromagnetic steel, magnetic particle inspection is the most direct way to find those cracks while they are still small, which is why the major equipment standards call for it.

The limit is the metal. MT works only on ferromagnetic material, and many oilfield parts are carbon or low-alloy steel, but corrosion-resistant alloys, stainless trim and some wellhead components are not magnetic. Those go to liquid penetrant testing for oilfield equipment. MT also finds only flaws open to the surface or just below it, so wall thickness and internal flaws are handled by ultrasonic testing for oilfield equipment.

Standards and who decides acceptance

Used drill stem elements are inspected and classified under API Recommended Practice 7G-2, with drill pipe built to API Specification 5DP and rotary connections to API Specification 7-1. Hoisting equipment is inspected under API Recommended Practice 8B, drilling and well-servicing structures under API Recommended Practice 4G, and the broader equipment under API Specification 7K. Wellhead and tree components follow API Specification 6A. Hooks and rigging hardware are covered by the ASME B30 series, for example B30.10 for hooks. The examination method itself follows ASME Section V, Article 7 and ASTM E1444, and our guide to Article 7 describes what a procedure states.

Some rig contractors specify a proprietary inspection standard such as DS-1. When the customer names one, we work to the customer’s document and its acceptance rules. In every case the customer decides whether an indication is rejectable; we report type, location, length and orientation. Technicians work under the company written practice based on ASNT SNT-TC-1A, with an ASNT Level III approving procedures and reviewing reports.

What we examine

  • Threaded connections. Pin and box threads, shoulders and the thread-root area on drill collars, subs, and heavy-weight and drill pipe tool joints, examined with fluorescent wet suspension when a dark enclosure is available.
  • Hoisting equipment. Hooks, elevators, links, bails, swivel bodies, crown and traveling block components and load-bearing welds. See magnetic particle inspection of lifting equipment.
  • Mast and substructure welds. Pad eyes, lifting lugs, brace connections and welded joints on drilling and well-servicing structures under API RP 4G practice.
  • Mud pump fluid ends. Cross-bore intersections, valve pockets and the surfaces around suction and discharge bores where fatigue cracks start.
  • Wellhead, spools and treating iron. Welds and machined features on forged bodies, hammer unions and flowline components.
  • Production skid and vessel welds. Nozzle attachments, lifting lugs and structural welds on separators, treaters and tanks, see magnetic particle weld inspection.
  • Castings and forgings. Surface condition of cast and forged bodies, see magnetic particle inspection of castings and forgings.

Technique for the equipment, not the textbook

Threads are the hardest geometry. A thread root is a groove, and the particle suspension tends to pool in it, so we use the technique the procedure specifies, often a central conductor or coil for circular and longitudinal fields, followed by careful drainage and rinsing. Direct contact methods are avoided on threaded connections wherever the customer’s document does not require them, because arcing at a contact point can burn the surface and create a new initiation site. Where yokes are used, the legs are placed so the field crosses the thread root, and the examination is repeated in a second orientation.

Fluorescent wet suspension is the sensitive choice for threads and fluid ends. It needs low ambient white light and ultraviolet-A light at about 1,000 microwatts per square centimeter at the part surface, so we bring a viewing tent or use a dark area in the yard or shop. Visible-colour wet particles on a contrasting paint are used for weld examination on structures, where the viewing area needs about 100 foot-candles of white light. Dry powder is useful outdoors on rough welds when conditions are windless and the part is dry; in rain, mud or cold, wet methods are the dependable ones.

Surface cleaning decides the result. Thread compound, mud, oil and rust block particle access, so we expect parts to be cleaned or we do the cleaning with approved solvents and brushes. Magnetized parts in the rack can attract ferrous debris, so after examination we demagnetize where the customer requires it, because residual fields can affect drilling instruments and downhole tools.

Fluid ends and pressure-cycled bodies

Mud and frac pump fluid ends are forged blocks with intersecting bores, and every pressure stroke concentrates stress where those bores meet. Cracks start at the cross-bore, at valve seat pockets and at the base of threads for retainers, and they often run parallel to the bore axis. The examination therefore needs access into the bore with a small-diameter light and a technique that magnetizes across the likely crack path, including a circular field by a central conductor where the procedure allows it. Cleaning matters most here: residue and scale in the bore hold particles and hide fine cracks. A fluid end that has been in service is cleaned, examined, and, where the customer requires it, demagnetized so metal debris does not collect on the next run.

The same logic applies to other pressure-cycled bodies: treating iron unions and swivel joints, plug valve bodies, wellhead spools and manifold blocks. The inspection schedule and the rejection criteria are the customer’s; our job is to show whether cracking exists and where.

Hoisting equipment in practice

Under API RP 8B, hoisting equipment is inspected at levels that rise with the severity of use and the time since the last inspection. The magnetic particle work belongs to the higher levels, where the unit is disassembled and critical surfaces are cleaned. Hooks are examined at the shank, the saddle and the throat; elevators at the bore, the latch area and the lift ears; swivels at the bail and the load-bearing shoulders. Pins and bushings are examined as separate items. Any repair weld on load-bearing parts needs a procedure from the equipment owner, and welds are examined after the specified heat treatment and cooling. We do not repair, we examine and report; any decision to retire, grind or weld belongs to the owner and the manufacturer.

Where oilfield MT jobs go wrong

Common errors include examining through paint or thread dope that is too thick, using one field direction only so cracks parallel to the field are missed, using too much current on a small part and burning contact points, and failing to document which surfaces were not examined. A fluid end checked in one direction can miss a crack along the bore. A weld inspected only from the crown can hide toe cracking under the ripples. Our reports state the directions used and the areas covered so a reviewer can see what the examination did and did not reach.

Hardened or heat-treated parts, such as tool joints with hard-banding or wear sleeves, can give non-relevant indications at the transitions. Experienced examiners classify those with confirmation passes and photographs, and refer to the Level III for decisions that fall outside the procedure.

MT in context with the other methods

Where each method fits on oilfield equipment
EquipmentMT findsWhere another method is needed
Drill stem threadsSurface fatigue cracks at rootsUT for body wall
Hoisting hardwareCracks at welds, shoulders and pinsUT for internal forging flaws
Mud pump fluid endBore-intersection fatigue cracksPT if the alloy is non-magnetic
Production skid weldToe and root-side surface cracksUT for embedded flaws
Stainless trimNothing; not ferromagneticPT

What the report contains

  • Customer, location, rig or lease, and equipment tag, serial or joint number.
  • Material, size and the governing standard or customer specification.
  • Procedure and revision, with the code edition.
  • Equipment and consumables: yoke or coil, particles, carrier, light readings for fluorescent work, field directions applied, and the lift or field check.
  • Surface condition, and any areas not examined and why.
  • Indications with position, length and orientation, with a photograph or sketch.
  • Examiner, qualification level and the report reviewer.
  • Demagnetization performed or not, if the customer requires it.

What to send for a quote

  1. Equipment list by type, size and quantity, with serial or joint numbers if available.
  2. The inspection standard in force, including any proprietary one the rig contractor requires.
  3. Whether parts are in the shop, racked in a yard or installed on a rig.
  4. Cleaning responsibility and surface condition.
  5. Site address, hazards such as H2S, and orientation or badging requirements.
  6. Report format and tagging convention.

Planning for oilfield schedules

Rig moves, rack inspections and shutdowns set the schedule. We ask for the plan and mobilize when the equipment is accessible and cleaned. Pad sites can be tight, wet or snow-covered, so we plan for a dark enclosure, power or battery equipment and shelter. Winter work on the northern plains and in Alaska needs heated enclosures for suspensions and parts at temperature, and summer heat in the Permian and Kern County affects couplant and suspension behavior. We follow gate control, H2S rules and rig safety orientation.

Where we work in the United States

  • Midland: Permian rigs, pump equipment yards and sour-service facilities.
  • Bakersfield: Kern County producing facilities and rig servicing under CalGEM oversight.
  • Oklahoma City: Anadarko drilling contractors and equipment yards.
  • Shreveport: Haynesville high-pressure well equipment.
  • Denver: DJ Basin rigs and production sites.
  • San Antonio: Eagle Ford rig and completion equipment.
  • Tulsa: drilling contractors, forgers and fabricators.
  • Anchorage: Alaska rigs where cold-weather enclosures are standard.
  • Houston: equipment manufacturers, repair shops and service companies.

What we do not do

We do not perform radiography in the United States, we do not run a fixed drill-stem inspection line, and we do not calculate remaining life or fitness for service. We do not offer techniques for crack sizing on this page. For the broader inspection scope see turnarounds and shutdowns and NDT technical procedure development.

Training your own technicians

Rig contractors and service companies can train their own people through MT Level 1 training and MT Level 2 training, with the magnetic particle simulator and oil and gas NDT training. The certificate comes from the employer, not from a course, and we help you write the practice behind it.

faq.q: What oilfield equipment benefits most from magnetic particle inspection?
faq.a: Threaded connections on drill stem elements, hoisting hardware, mast and substructure welds and mud pump fluid ends all fail by surface-initiated fatigue, so MT finds problems on ferromagnetic steel before parts fail.

faq.q: Do you follow API RP 7G-2 and RP 8B?
faq.a: We work to API RP 7G-2, API RP 8B or API RP 4G where the customer specifies them, using ASME Section V, Article 7 and ASTM E1444 for the method. The customer’s document governs scope and acceptance.

faq.q: Can you inspect drill pipe connections in the yard?
faq.a: Yes, when joints are racked and cleaned. We examine pin and box threads, shoulders and thread roots, then report indications by joint number. We do not run a fixed drill-stem inspection line.

faq.q: Why does MT sometimes need a dark enclosure?
faq.a: Fluorescent particles need ultraviolet light and very low ambient white light, so in daylight we use a tent or hood. Visible-colour particles on weld surfaces need strong white light instead.
DS-1 is a proprietary standard. When a customer specifies it or another proprietary standard, we follow the customer’s document and acceptance rules for the magnetic particle work we perform.

faq.q: Can MT inspect stainless steel wellhead components?
faq.a: Not if the alloy is austenitic, because it is not ferromagnetic. We use liquid penetrant testing on non-magnetic parts, and check magnetic response before choosing the method.

faq.q: Who accepts or rejects an indication?
faq.a: The customer or its engineer does, applying the standard in its specification. We report type, location, length and orientation and note any non-relevant indications and why we classified them that way.

faq.q: What do you need from us to quote an oilfield MT job?
faq.a: An equipment list with sizes and quantities, the governing standard, where the parts are, who cleans them, site address, hazards such as H2S, orientation requirements and the report format.

faq.q: Do you offer radiography for oilfield welds?
faq.a: No. Radiography in the United States is licensed under NRC or Agreement State rules and is outside our scope. We perform MT, PT and UT and can have a Level III review your procedures.
